entries.title: Cherise Saywell wins national short story award for ‘tender’ tale of a child facing violence – read an extract here
entries.summary: The Edinburgh-based writer takes £15,000 prize for Ditto, a ‘beautifully told’ story about domestic abuse in a small Australian townRead an extract from Ditto belowEdinburgh-based writer Cherise Saywell has won this year’s BBC national short story award for a “tender” and “taut” story about a young boy caught in the midst of domestic violence.Saywell was announced as the winner of the £15,000 awar
entries.content:
Edinburgh-based writer Cherise Saywell has won this year’s BBC national short story award for a “tender” and “taut” story about a young boy caught in the midst of domestic violence.

Saywell was announced as the winner of the £15,000 award, run in collaboration with the University of Cambridge, at a ceremony held at BBC Broadcasting House on Tuesday evening.

Set in an isolated Australian town inspired by the place where Saywell grew up, the story follows a boy nicknamed Ditto as he grapples with what to do when his mother is threatened, eventually finding the courage to use a public telephone box to call the police.

“Taut and beautifully crafted, tender and deeply rooted in one dusk evening and one small town, Saywell’s story writing is assured and true and we are absolutely delighted that Ditto is this year’s winner,” said Di Speirs, chair of the judging panel.

Saywell, who was born and raised in Australia and has lived in Scotland since 1996, said she wanted to explore “how children experience violence, when they have no words for the things they are experiencing”.

“They feel love and fear and responsibility all at the same time, but have no name for what’s happening around them,” she said.

Saywell is the author of two novels, Desert Fish and Twitcher. Her short fiction has won the Pindrop short story award, the Mslexia short story prize and the VS Pritchett prize, and she has also been shortlisted for the Bristol prize and Asham award. She works for the Royal Literary Fund.

Saywell beat an all-female shortlist that included Irish writer Caoilinn Hughes, Lucy Caldwell, who won the award in 2021, biographer and novelist Laura Beatty, and Merryn Glover. Each of the authors shortlisted for the short story award receives £600. Their stories appear in an anthology published by Comma Press, and are available to listen to on BBC Sounds.

“Full of vivid descriptions, mounting tensions, and a compelling character, Ditto is a moving reminder of how much life a short story can hold and what’s simmering beneath the surface. It really is beautifully told,” said Dr Yvonne Battle-Felton, academic director for creative writing at the University of Cambridge.

Speirs was joined on the judging panel by 2022 winner Saba Sams and two former shortlisted writers, Tahmima Anam and Will Eaves, and Costa best first novel award winner, Andrew Michael Hurley.

The BBC national short story award is one of the UK’s major prizes for a single short story. Previous winners include Sarah Hall, Jonathan Buckley, Lucy Caldwell, Ingrid Persaud and Saba Sams. Last year’s award was won by Colwill Brown for You Cannot Thread a Moving Needle.

The winner of the young writer’s award, open to 14 to 18-year-olds, was also announced at the ceremony. Eloise Barrett, a 17-year-old sixth former from Birmingham, won for Bloodshed in Rafah, a “heartwrenching” story about the reality of a childhood affected by war.

Ditto

After he made the call, Ditto ran from the public phone booth at the top of the street, past all seven houses, including his own, until he reached the place where the road ran out – the dead end, his father called it. He slowed there, as if he’d arrived somewhere he was expected. Beyond him, concealed by the night, was a sort of no man’s land – scrub and then a rocky embankment, and after that the railroad tracks. The sun was gone nearly an hour and lights had come on in houses and along the streets. Beneath Ditto’s sandshoes, the bitumen was gritty and loose, so he shifted his feet with great care, picked his way beyond the verge to where there was a patch of lantana. Crouching, he tucked himself into it and put his hand to his watch. It was his best thing, won in a competition. He slid his finger over the button that would illuminate its face but did not press for fear that this small light might reveal him. Instead, tensing his muscles, he listened to the night for a brief, frightened moment, then plugged his ears with his fingers and looked east, in the direction from where the police car would approach, if it came at all. The train would emerge from the same patch of blackness at 7.32pm. It passed by every night at the same time, on its way to Sydney.

“Twenty minutes,” the woman had told him at the booth. It was the last thing she’d said before she left him there. “Twenty minutes, I reckon, if you call now and say what I told you. They’ll turn up before the train goes past.”

The first thing she’d said (after she’d rapped on the glass door) was his birth name, not “Ditto”. “Your mother’s Lonnie, right?”

Ditto hadn’t replied right away. He knew the woman lived directly opposite the phone booth, but he’d never seen her speak to his mother, not on the street, nor in the corner shop, nor anywhere else. He was aware it looked as if he was up to no good, mucking about in the booth. It could be a novelty, especially if you didn’t have a phone at home, and sometimes even if you did. There were numbers you could dial, some for free, just for the fun of it. Indeed, an automated voice had been chanting in his ear – at the third stroke, it will be … Only, he’d not been mucking about. It was none of her business anyway. He’d adjusted his stance and stared at the dial, willing her to walk away. Instead, she’d hoisted the door open, and he’d almost dropped the receiver; in his panic, he’d banged his head on the glass. But then she’d put her hands up, palms out, and something about the way she did that made him want to fall into her arms. It was an awful feeling.

“Shhh,” she’d said, as if he was a wild thing trapped in that cramped space. “Shhh.” He’d remained perfectly still, clutching the receiver in his left hand, holding it away from his face, the automated voice now an articulated buzz – at the third stroke … at the third stroke …. She’d have heard it. Oh, the shame, and something else, indecipherable, a knot of it deep inside himself, a wave of heat rising from his neck and into his face; he’d looked away from those eyes of hers – had he not, they might have burned through his skin and exposed the ugly inside of him.

“She gave it to you, didn’t she,” the woman had said, indicating his now-closed fist, the coin. “Your mother.” He’d watched his feet, pulling the receiver to his chest, saying nothing. But she was unperturbed. “I’ve seen you here. I’ve seen you here plenty of times with a coin in your hand.” She’d pointed at the phone. “But I don’t reckon you make the call.”

Hunched in the lantana, Ditto’s stomach grew tight now, thinking of it, and his mouth watered like it had in that moment, when he was certain he would be sick.

  • A full audio recording of Ditto is

    available on BBC Sounds.

entries.title: The Fall of the West by Owen Jones review – a bracing history of the changing world order
entries.summary: A journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreach Like many Britons born in the 1980s, the journalist and Guardian columnist Owen Jones came of age with Tony Blair’s platitudes ringing in his ears. Politics at the turn of the millennium was a story of temporary dispensations mistaken for eternal truths: the definitive triumph of free market ideology; US military s
entries.content:
Like many Britons born in the 1980s, the journalist and Guardian columnist Owen Jones came of age with Tony Blair’s platitudes ringing in his ears. Politics at the turn of the millennium was a story of temporary dispensations mistaken for eternal truths: the definitive triumph of free market ideology; US military supremacy; a rules-based global order. As Jones recounts in his new book, these certainties would come crashing down over the next quarter of a century amid a succession of economic failures, foreign policy disasters and political crises.

Indeed, “the west” itself – as a shorthand for the US plus the wealthier western European nations – feels almost quaint today, given the increasing unilateralism of the administration in Washington. But in the 2000s it was part of the lexicon, as if the hemisphere were a political actor in its own right. Revisiting the US-led wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, we are reminded not just of their horrific death tolls (totalling half a million, by conservative estimates) but also their total strategic failure; the 2021 evacuation of Kabul airport, Jones writes, was “among the starkest images of American decline yet broadcast to the world”.

In addition to destabilising the region, these interventions weakened the foundations of the international legal system. As Jones points out, a precedent was set when Nato bombed Yugoslavia without UN security council authorisation in 1999; the 2003 invasion of Iraq, also without authorisation, further undermined the UN. So when Vladimir Putin subsequently invaded Ukraine on his own dubious pretext, western objections could be dismissed as hypocrisy. Perhaps the most ignominious example of western indifference to the international rule of law was Keir Starmer’s limp assertion that Israel had the “right” to cut off water and electricity to 2 million civilians in Gaza – a war crime – in retaliation for Hamas’s attacks on 7 October 2023.

Alongside these geopolitical catastrophes, Jones tells a story of domestic decline, of western economies built on chronic insecurity and precarious employment. In the 2000s, Thatcherite policies pursued by New Labour fleeced the public: “Essential services [were] turned into assets designed to generate returns. Passengers paid more for overcrowded trains. Rivers and seas were fouled while water companies loaded themselves with debt and paid out dividends.” Then came the 2008 financial crisis and the bankers’ bailout, paid for by austerity. In Britain and elsewhere, Jones notes a “correlation between the inability of centrist governments to tackle economic decline in any meaningful way, and the rise of the far right”.

The book is interspersed with snippets of interviews with an assortment of eyewitnesses, journalists, scholars and activists. They include the director of Iraq national museum in Baghdad, a former Lehman Brothers employee, a former head of the Afghan Red Crescent, the Greek economist Yanis Varoufakis, and the conservative commentator Andrew Sullivan, a repentant cheerleader for the Iraq war, who admits: “I was wrong on the major issues, on the morality of it and the practicality of it and the reason for it.”

Much of this terrain – Bush and Blair’s wars, the financial crash, the populist surge – has been extensively covered. The average well-informed reader will learn nothing new, but it is bracing to see what was once the news cycle take its place in the sweep of history, and Jones’s focus on free-market fundamentalism provides a compelling through-line. He suggests the second Trump administration, in all its cynical venality, is “the logical endpoint” of that philosophy. And he reminds us that the aggressive privatisation of the Russian economy in the 1990s brought terrible economic hardship which ultimately fuelled Putin’s revanchist nationalism.

For decades, electorates have been mis-sold a fanatical ideology: the prerogatives of the private sector must override the collective interest, and anything less is tantamount to Stalinism. This remains orthodoxy, but the rise to prominence of Zohran Mamdani, the avowedly socialist mayor of New York, offers a glimmer of hope to those who, like Jones, would prefer a society built on “common provision, democratic power, mutual obligation and the recognition that our fates are bound together”.

entries.title: Stations by Louise Kennedy review – a superb follow-up to Trespasses
entries.summary: This tale of broken hearts and broken people moves from the Troubles of 1980s Northern Ireland to an unforgiving London of squats and payphonesLouise Kennedy’s first novel, Trespasses, was one of those rare triumphs, a debut that was not only rapturously received by critics but adored by readers around the world. A story of forbidden love set during the Troubles in 1970s Belfast, it was an interna
entries.content:
Louise Kennedy’s first novel, Trespasses, was one of those rare triumphs, a debut that was not only rapturously received by critics but adored by readers around the world. A story of forbidden love set during the Troubles in 1970s Belfast, it was an international bestseller, translated into more than 20 languages. It was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize and scooped debut fiction of the year at the British Book awards. A four-part television adaptation with Gillian Anderson aired last autumn on Channel 4.

Inevitably Kennedy found herself lauded as an overnight success – much was made of her 30-year career as a professional chef – but in fact she had been writing short stories for a decade and to considerable acclaim; her first collection, The End of the World Is a Cul de Sac, was published in 2021. Included in that book was Belladonna, the story of Róisín, a young girl from Belfast who moves south with her mother and, ostracised by her new classmates, becomes friendly with the couple who live across the road. Like Briony Tallis in Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the prickly and precociously bright Róisín misinterprets the dynamic of her neighbours’ marriage to disastrous effect.

It is a sucker-punch of a story, conjuring in a few restrained pages the violent insecurity and self-absorption of early adolescence. What a joy, then, to rediscover Róisín in the opening pages of Stations, Kennedy’s blisteringly good second novel. It is 1982 and Róisín, still very much the outsider from the north, strikes up a fierce and unexpected friendship with Red, a boy with a reputation for trouble who is “spoken about in giddy whispers at school”. Róisín’s father, a drinker, has moved with his new wife to London. Red’s family is dysfunctional in ways Róisín only vaguely understands, but which come to a head when Red finds himself on the wrong side of the law. Unable to stay, Red bolts to London. It is a year before Róisín, visiting her father for Christmas, finds herself caught up with him once again, the pull he exerts on her impossible to resist.

The novel traces the warp and weft of their relationship over the next 25 years. Structured like a sporadically kept diary, clusters of dated entries disrupted by long gaps, it has echoes of David Nicholls’s One Day; but Kennedy’s London is altogether grimmer and more brutal, a city of squats and gas heaters and not enough change for the payphone. Her people are also more damaged, an Irish diaspora fractured by displacement, scarred not only by poverty and violence and addiction but by shame and loss. “Can you not feel it?” Red asks Róisín when, walking through London, they pass the site of the old Millbank prison. “All those wretched lives layered up underneath us.” Kennedy’s émigrés flee the old country, they build new lives, construct new families, but they carry the weight of the past always with them. However far they travel, they can never escape from themselves.

Kennedy moved to London herself as a young woman and evokes the 1980s city with almost hallucinogenic precision, but her greater power lies in her remarkable humanity. Her characters are messy, flawed, often shatteringly self-destructive but, mapped with her fierce compassion, they march straight off the page. As a teenager Róisín is bolshy and obstreperous; she is also funny and filthy and generous and agonisingly vulnerable. As she gets older, she gets better – sometimes – at managing herself but she never really changes. The way Kennedy conjures her, we do not want her to.

Stations is at its heart a love story, a furious, tender, potty-mouthed paean to loyalty and generosity of spirit. It is also an elegy to a generation of lost Irish boys, a heartbreaking testament to the violence and fear passed down from father to son. In its title, Stations acknowledges the transience of the diasporic experience, the trains and boats and coaches, but, steeped as the book is in an in-the-bone Catholicism (one particularly powerful scene has Róisín unable to bring herself to shake Red’s father’s hand at Mass), it carries too the idea of the Stations of the Cross, the 14 images of Jesus on the day of his Crucifixion.

In Trespasses, the teacher Cushla, studying the Stations during the Easter Sunday sermon, reckons Jesus “a ringer for James Taylor”. In Stations, it is tempting to see the elusive and charismatic Red, “loping along in [Róisín’s] father’s coat like an itinerant preacher”, as a Christ figure, offering a kind of redemption through his suffering. Can cycles of anguish or neglect ever be broken? Is love in all its frustrating insufficiency enough to save us? Kennedy’s novel is too subtle and clear-eyed to offer easy answers, but her questions will burn themselves into your heart.

entries.title: Range by Dorthe Nors review – an astrophysicist at odds with reality
entries.summary: In the Danish writer’s latest novel, an eminent scientist withdraws to the countrysideWhen Gunn Haven, an eminent professor of astrophysics at an urban university, moves to rural Denmark, she tells a local newspaper: “It’s to do with the sky.” From the outset of Range, Danish author Dorthe Nors’s fifth full-length novel, it is apparent this is not the whole truth. Soon after arriving, Gunn is comp
entries.content:
When Gunn Haven, an eminent professor of astrophysics at an urban university, moves to rural Denmark, she tells a local newspaper: “It’s to do with the sky.” From the outset of Range, Danish author Dorthe Nors’s fifth full-length novel, it is apparent this is not the whole truth. Soon after arriving, Gunn is compelled to trespass along a nearby track to look at a farmhouse with collapsed gable walls, her curiosity driven by personal interest rather than scientific inquiry. A woman pulls up in a dark blue BMW. She is dressed in “hunter’s camouflage, fleshy-faced. And ponytailed. Weapon raised: a phone, filming Gunn.” Gunn reluctantly retreats.

Gunn is distracted by this woman, Krista, who works at the local potato flour factory. Gunn should be working on a general introduction to astrophysics, “the Work”. Instead, the Professor finds herself wondering what “Gable Woman” would do if she came to “the Institute”, where Gunn researches “light from the oldest galaxies”. She would draw a dick on a blackboard, Gunn imagines, “with a small titillated smile”. Gunn is more generous to promising young scientists. She pays for a former student to travel to America. Closer to home, she begins to help Jenny, the teenage daughter of her hairdresser, with a school project on black holes. Jenny is an “uneducated creature” who smells “faintly of iron”, with a “faint red to the cheeks, from shyness or cold. Oddly sexless, and she had been here before, but with her mother.”

The construction of that sentence – from fragments and obtrusive conjunctions – is typical of Caroline Waight’s English translation of Range. The novel’s imagery is equally difficult to understand. During a lecture, Gunn thinks: “I’m coated in saliva.” Speculating on how a colony on Mars might develop, she says: “second generation: identical glasses and spit”.

Nors’s previous novel translated into English, Mirror, Shoulder, Signal, is also about a woman whose interior world is at odds with external reality. The novel, shortlisted for the 2017 International Booker prize, follows Sonja, a middle-aged translator of Swedish crime novels, as she embarks on driving lessons. Sonja makes a living finding just the right words for acts of graphic violence. The novel’s subtle humour comes in the juxtaposition between the details of this violence and the mundane challenges of Sonja’s life, such as learning to use a gated stick shift. In Range, the incongruity between Gunn and those around her feels darker and more cryptic. Gunn receives a dead bird in her post box and a “For Sale” sign is moved close to her house. These hostile acts trigger memories of Gunn’s early life, which filter through her studies of the universe’s earliest light. Gunn’s mother died in a traffic accident. Her childhood with her father was poor but loving, with “moments of equations so long they went beyond any greasy cooker hood”. This might explain why, in adult life, Gunn is so concerned with the celestial that she fails to understand more local phenomena, such as other people.

Gunn’s thinking, however, is improbably imprecise. “The Work” is jumbled and vague. Gunn imagines evolution will soon mean “we’ll be born with Vaseline glands”. If this construction is distracting, the following description is dismaying: “But she didn’t get that far: she heard the car before she saw it. Rather like with thunder, and she turned back to the living room, crouched.” Gunn, an astrophysicist so renowned that her moving house is reported in the local newspaper, seems to believe that thunder is heard before lightning is seen.

Gunn is interested in Jane Austen’s novel Persuasion because “the word was nice”. She buys a copy of a Danish translation and is disappointed to find a glaring mistake on page one (“1810” had become “1801”). “Such sloppiness was unforgivable, and the sentences trickled on and on, riddled with mistakes no doubt.” She impatiently flips to the end of the book and decides that the story’s moral is “to listen to Lady Russell”, a “seemingly childless” widow who is “like a mother” to the central character, Anne. There is an obvious parallel between Lady Russell and Gunn, who we learn is both mentor and mentee, taken in by the woman from whom she inherited the house. The scenes of awkward intimacy between Gunn and Jenny are the tender heart of Range, but they are wrapped in a predictable plot, leading to an unconvincing altercation with “brutish” Krista that confirms Gunn’s prejudices about rural life. I kept thinking of a line from Mirror, Shoulder, Signal, in which Sonja comments on the many people who feel forced to move from the countryside to Copenhagen: “Shaming the provinces is just a covert form of deportation.”

entries.title: Deep into the Sixties: Britain 1965-66 by David Kynaston review – a tour de force of popular history
entries.summary: From the Beatles and the World Cup to racism and homophobia, the latest instalment in Kynaston’s series captures a society in the throes of changeIn February 1965, the civil rights activist Malcolm X visited Smethwick, in the Midlands, where the Conservative-run council was planning to buy up houses to stop the area becoming a “coloured ghetto”. He wanted to see how bad the racism was and he exper
entries.content:
In February 1965, the civil rights activist Malcolm X visited Smethwick, in the Midlands, where the Conservative-run council was planning to buy up houses to stop the area becoming a “coloured ghetto”. He wanted to see how bad the racism was and he experienced it first-hand when refused service in a pub. White residents thought his visit a “disgusting” intrusion. Nine days later, back in the US, he was shot dead.

Britain in the mid-60s is associated with Carnaby Street, the Beatles and miniskirts, not racism. But what Black people endured, from a colour bar on property to the abuse of Leeds United winger Albert Johanneson as a “golliwog”, is no less a period marker than Harold Wilson’s pipe, Twiggy’s haircut, Mary Whitehouse’s clean-up TV campaign and Bob Dylan’s use of an electric guitar. David Kynaston doesn’t underplay the excitements of the period. But he rightly emphasises that the rotten old 50s – patriarchal, homophobic, class-divided and bigoted – wouldn’t just fade away.

His mammoth project, a history of Britain from 1945‑79, is now past halfway. He originally expected this volume to continue to 1967. In the event it covers just 18 months, from February 1965 to July 1966, and (with notes) runs to nearly 700 pages. The challenge is to balance an in-depth account of politics, economics, industry, education and culture with personal stories of what it was like to be there: the food you ate, the clothes you wore, the films you saw. The sources he draws on range from statistical surveys and sociological reports to political biographies, personal diaries and the grouchy letters of Philip Larkin. No living historian is as comprehensive.

With much to accommodate, he relies on the semicolon for day-by-day narration: “At a Monday morning cabinet session…;” “later that afternoon …;” “on the box the same evening …;” “next morning in Manchester … ;” and so on. The sentences are long but full of humour and never dull. The high point comes with a “freewheelin’, mid-60s play list” (duly abbreviated here) that takes up five pages:

Multi-flavoured Golden Wonder crisps displacing Smith’s plain; one-third of new marriages now civil marriages; pubs reluctantly installing fruit machines; Jimmy Hill’s Sky-Blue revolution at Coventry City; AA patrols no longer required to salute; picture rails, seen as dust traps, removed en masse from Victorian and Edwardian houses; Boots from 1965 at last consenting to sell condoms; arrival of open-plan offices; arrival, too, of the hot drinks vending machine; no car more iconic of modernity than the Mini Cooper …

As well as giving us snippets from daily life and reminding us how nasty the 60s could be (Ian Brady, Myra Hindley and the Kray brothers), Kynaston devotes chapters to larger-scale cultural shifts, chief among them in education. Harold Wilson dreamed of “a Britain in which anyone can get to the top on merit and ability, not on social or family connections”, and the shift to comprehensive schools was integral to that. Grammar schools resisted, public schools clung on to their independence, and refusenik local authorities caricatured the change as a Nazi-like conspiracy designed to “tyrannise the minds of the young” and create “animal farms” run by state commissars. But Anthony Crosland pushed hard for the reform and it did Labour no harm in the March 1966 general election, which kept them in power with a majority of 97 seats.

Polytechnics arrived too – 30 of them over the following eight years, along with the Open University. This wasn’t quite the age of social mobility it’s cracked up to be. Most children still left school at 15. Whereas 50% of high-school graduates in the US went on to university, it was still less than 6% in the UK. But expansion was under way. And many of the era’s famous names – David Bailey, Albert Finney, Michael Caine, Jean Shrimpton, Harold Evans, Terence Stamp, Cilla Black and Lulu – had working-class roots.

Kynaston also explores the rebuilding of cities: slum clearances, tower blocks and (in the words of the song by pop band Unit 4 Plus 2), concrete and clay. It was a peak time for high rises, with whole streets destroyed (as if wartime bombing had resumed) and millions of people displaced to new estates. Some were grateful to escape the damp and squalor of the houses they’d been in; many were not: “I’d rather have a tent on the moors.” Kynaston detects “a certain residual arrogance” in the architects and planners. The pendulum would gradually swing against a “dim-witted adulation of Le Corbusier”, but until then the vogue was for streets in the sky.

Happily, there was also a vogue for liberalisation: of birth control, abortion law, consensual sex between men, and greater opportunities for women. All were much needed: homosexuality was widely vilified; the Factories Act forbade women to do night shifts and only 80 of 1,707 candidates at the election were female; family planning clinics wouldn’t see young, unmarried women, one of whom asked agony aunt Marjorie Proops: “If a girl has intercourse, and then has nothing to do with boys for a year, can she have become a virgin again?” More surprising is to find that half the workforce in 1966 was already in the service industry and that the City of London was a hub of global power long before the 1980s.

The book’s likeliest readers will be those alive at the time, whose memories will be triggered by what was new (the Post Office Tower, microwaves, Laker Airways), what needed phasing out (bottom-pinching, outdoor loos, “the brain-damaging heaviness” of leather footballs) and what songs, plays, films and television programmes had to say about contemporary life. Kynaston quotes generously from reviews, many of them more robust than you find today (“pretentious bunkum”, “inane, asinine, witless”); the BBC’s brilliant Wednesday Play series infuriated audiences and even the Beatles were denounced when awarded MBEs: “All they do is exploit a basic jungle rhythm for money.” A younger audience may be struck by the parallels between then and now: a Labour prime minister from the north, economic strife, the US in a pointless war, hostility to immigrants. We’re not facing devaluation of the pound, as Harold Wilson was. Still, the continuities stretch forward as well as back.

The last section of the book is a tour de force, interspersing Kenneth Wolstenholme’s commentary on the World Cup final (“Four minutes now left to play and the crowd biting fingernails down to the knuckles”) with the reactions of those watching on television, among them young Laurence Marks, the finest of the diarists quoted in the book, who stood to lose £2/12 shillings on a bet if England won, and Kynaston himself, on his 15th birthday: “I retreat upstairs to my bedroom and play a side of a Nancy Sinatra album, reckoning it will see both me and England through.” It did. The match was a triumph and so is the book. But spare a thought for the 6,000-strong crowd in Devon who’d paid to see the Kinks perform that night. The band stayed in London till the match was over and, arriving two hours late at 11.45pm, were allowed to play for just 10 minutes.

entries.title: Tomi Adeyemi on the film of her hit novel Children of Blood and Bone: ‘I don’t plan to watch it’
entries.summary: Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novelThere is a photograph of Tomi Adeyemi staring out from the cover of her new novel, The Siren. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the vi
entries.content:
There is a photograph of Tomi Adeyemi staring out from the cover of her new novel, The Siren. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the viewer. “It’s terrifying – like the Mona Lisa, staring at you everywhere,” she says, laughing.

Using an author portrait on the cover of a novel is highly unusual, and a decision that Adeyemi says is a statement of ownership. After 12 years spent inside the world of Children of Blood and Bone – the first book in the YA trilogy that made her a literary star and its film adaptation which has become a source of profound distress – Adeyemi wanted this book to belong unmistakably to her.

“It was an intense choice, and I think it’s because I needed people to see me in this one,” she says. “I’ve had so much success, but it was also done in a way where so many people’s interpretations were put on to who I was.”

The recent public fallout from the forthcoming film adaptation may have drawn attention, but the 33-year-old Nigerian American author had already spent much of her adult life being watched. Children of Blood and Bone, her 2018 debut, became a publishing phenomenon, netting a major seven-figure deal and debuting at No 1 on the New York Times young adult bestseller list. Its story of Zélie, a young woman fighting to restore magic to the kingdom of Orïsha, was inspired by West African mythology and offered something Adeyemi had craved as a child: a dark-skinned Black girl at the centre of an epic fantasy.

The success brought its own mythology. Adeyemi was not merely a successful young writer; she became, she feels, a symbol of what the next generation of Black YA literature might be, something she felt the weight of acutely.

“I felt pressure to be the perfect dark-skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’,” she says. “This was the biggest YA book deal in history, not just for a female or Black author. And so few of us are given a shot at all, so for the last 12 years there’s been this sense of carrying everyone.”

Readers would tell her what the book had meant to their children. “You have no idea what this did for me,” they would say. Such responses were moving, but also difficult to know what to do with.

Now, with The Siren, Adeyemi has moved from epic fantasy to something more contemporary. The standalone novel follows Emery, a Black student arriving at Dartmouth College determined to leave her troubled past behind. She is drawn into a mysterious sorority of “Sirens” and desperate to fit in. In some ways, Adeyemi says, the book is deeply personal. “[Emery] is my inner teen,” Adeyemi says. “I just want to give her a hug.”

She may have found success, but in the beginning Adeyemi’s career never looked certain. She wrote her first story at five – a Parent Trap fan fiction because, she says, she “wanted a twin and a horse”. She then spent years trying not to become a writer. Her parents had moved to Chicago from Nigeria in their early 20s, and Adeyemi grew up with the ethos of relentless achievement that often comes with first-generation immigrants – one that does not take kindly to creative pursuits. She considered medicine, investment banking and consulting, but kept coming back to writing. “Being called to be an artist is terrifying,” she says. “It’s not a logical choice.”

After studying English at Harvard, Adeyemi won a fellowship to study West African mythology and culture in Salvador, Brazil, an experience that would later inspire Children of Blood and Bone. She moved to California and began working part time at a film production company in Los Angeles, alongside writing her first novel.

That first attempt took four and a half years to write and received 63 rejections. She decided to drop the manuscript and wrote Children of Blood and Bone instead. When it was finally published in 2018 it quickly became one of the most talked about YA novels of the year. For a writer who had spent years being turned down, the speed and scale of what followed were dizzying. “I never really adjusted, because there was so much work still to do,” she says. “It’s been 12 to 14 years of intense grinding.”

And then came the film. On paper, it was the stuff of a writer’s dreams: her novel was to be transformed into a major Hollywood production, with an impossibly starry cast including Viola Davis, Idris Elba, Regina King, Damson Idris, Amandla Stenberg and Cynthia Erivo, premiering in January 2027. Adeyemi co-wrote the screenplay, but as the adaptation progressed, she became increasingly unhappy with the process.

In July, Adeyemi posted a five-minute video on TikTok in which she described the adaptation process as “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”. She said she had left the set “hyperventilating and sobbing”, and that afterwards she experienced severe physical pain and panic attacks. “I never want to hear about this project again,” she said.

She says she had little hesitation about speaking publicly. “I understood that if I didn’t speak up, I couldn’t move forward,” she explains. “I can’t really worry about the response, because I don’t have to live with how people respond to me – I have to live with me, every day.”

When I ask what exactly happened on set, however, Adeyemi hesitates. “I won’t go into the specifics,” she says carefully. “[But] the whole journey of the trilogy and the adaptation felt biblical … It took all of me.”

There has, though, been public discussion around the film’s casting of Amandla Stenberg, who is mixed race, and questions around colourism: Stenberg’s character is described in the book as having “dark copper skin”. Adeyemi’s July TikTok also appeared to show messages she sent to Stenberg in February 2025, around the time Stenberg responded to the colourism backlash, telling the actor: “Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me.”

When I ask Adeyemi whether she wants to clarify anything about the casting, she demurs. “With a film, the director makes every decision,” she says. “With my book I can talk about every choice down to the commas, because that’s truly in my hands. So there’s nothing for me to add, other than the clarity that these aren’t my choices.”

She is clear, though, about one thing. When I ask her if she would ever adapt another one of her books for screen she responds simply: “Never.” She has no desire to watch the upcoming film either. “I still don’t plan to watch it, but it’s not really for me to watch,” she says.

Instead, she is trying to leave the world of Children of Blood and Bone behind, and focus on what she has achieved. “I’m proud of my strength, resilience, and grace,” she says.

She is also proud of what she believes her debut set in motion: the fact that she can now walk into a bookshop and see shelves of dark-skinned protagonists across fantasy, romance, thrillers and mysteries. “The girls who grew up after me will never have that experience,” she says. As her publisher told her: “You changed things.”

entries.content:
In Dr Seuss’s Green Eggs and Ham, the relentlessly upbeat Sam-I-Am spends the entire book badgering a grouchy, nameless narrator into tasting the eponymous dish. He cycles through one inventive but futile pitch after another – in a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, on a train, in the rain – until the narrator, caving just to get some peace, tastes the dish and discovers he loves it. When my son was growing up, “Green Eggs and Ham” was my shorthand for telling him he was avoiding something he’d love if he only tried it.

Of course, not every experience we fear or dread turns out to be a delicious surprise. Misery is an inescapable part of the human condition. We can’t avoid it, yet people try their hardest anyway. We cling to hope even when a situation is hopeless. We push painful thoughts out of mind rather than confront them. We struggle to control things that cannot be changed. And we go to sometimes self-destructive lengths to protect our pride from even the tiniest pinprick. These strategies may sometimes spare us pain in the moment. But while they are intended to promote (or at least preserve) our happiness, over time they have the perverse result of making us much more miserable.

Consider relationships. Declining to chat with the talkative person sitting next to you on a plane avoids one obvious downside – getting stuck in a boring conversation you can’t gracefully exit. But as psychologist Nicholas Epley shows in an extensive body of research, doing this again and again quietly robs us of interactions we might have found genuinely rewarding, though we’ll never know what we missed.

The same instinct to protect ourselves can become more destructive in close relationships, when the misery that we fear is rejection. People who are “rejection sensitive” tend to expect the worst and see signs of the coming apocalypse even in ambiguous behaviour, like an unanswered text message. When they think they see rejection coming, they try to avoid it by rejecting first – responding with hostility or pulling away from their partner in a self-defeating effort to protect themselves. As a result, behaviour that was meant to ward off rejection ends up provoking it.

In my own research, I surveyed a large sample of adults, asking whether they take too many risks, too few, or roughly the right amount – both overall and across key areas such as work, health and relationships. The results were striking. About half felt they took the right amount of risk. But among the rest, the overwhelming majority felt they took too few – and the reason they gave, again and again, was a desire to avoid miserable emotions like fear and regret.

One of the great engines of misery is “counterfactual thinking”: our mental habit of imagining how things might have gone differently. While we have the capacity to imagine better and worse outcomes, research shows that we are much more likely to dwell on how things could have been better than to consider how they could have been worse. Such “upward counterfactuals” – the job offer we didn’t take, the romantic connection we didn’t pursue – tend to leave us feeling regretful and dissatisfied with the reality we actually have. This asymmetry punishes those who assiduously avoid every opportunity that might result in pain or heartbreak, because such avoidance inevitably creates a stockpile of upward counterfactuals, all the roads not taken. Psychologists distinguish regrets of commission from regrets of omission; it’s the latter – the things we could have done but didn’t – that haunt us longest.

We don’t only avoid misery by avoiding risky behaviour; a whole separate category of avoidance happens purely in the mind. We reach for distraction, numbing, and busyness to keep from thinking about what causes us pain. But you cannot anaesthetise sadness without anaesthetising everything nearby. Emotional systems don’t come with a dial that turns down grief while leaving joy untouched; suppress one and the whole range tends to flatten.

The practised avoider often ends up not happy, exactly, but flat – free of acute suffering, perhaps, but also missing the intensity, curiosity, and aliveness that make the good parts of life feel good. This flatness is easy to mistake for equanimity, since it doesn’t announce itself as pain. The protagonist in Stefan Zweig’s story Fantastic Night lives this numbness for years, until one reckless act cracks it open – and what rushes back in isn’t relief but a flood of feeling, the discovery that his calm had been an absence, rather than peace.

Research on physical pain finds, surprisingly, that focusing on pain can diminish its intensity more effectively than trying to distract from it – and there are parallel, if somewhat more mixed, findings for negative emotions generally. One line of inquiry shows that “affect labelling” – simply putting feelings into words – dampens neural reactions to distress. Another set of studies finds that people instructed to accept a negative emotion, rather than suppress it, recover faster, both emotionally and physiologically.

None of this is an argument for deliberately courting misery, or for treating pain as good in itself. But unhappiness-avoidance, adopted as an organising life principle rather than an occasional and reasonable caution, is self-undermining. It reduces the kinds of experiences available to us, including those of the “Green Eggs and Ham” variety that may prove incredibly meaningful.

My father, born a German Jew, spent part of the second world war in a French prisoner of war camp. He and the small pack of close friends he made there were hungry enough to dig up worms for food and chew on shoe leather. But he once told me that, due to the companionship and challenge of that ordeal, it was the peak experience of his life. Avoidance of misery rests on a false premise about how happiness actually works. The person who spends a life dodging unhappiness does not arrive, in the end, at a life free from misery. Unhappiness avoided is not happiness gained, but more often just misery in disguise.

George Loewenstein is university professor of economics and psychology at Carnegie Mellon, and author of The Opposite of Happiness (William Collins).

Further reading

Better in Every Sense by Norman Farb and Zindel Segal (Yellow Kite, £20)

The Antidote by Oliver Burkeman (Vintage, £12.99)

Full Catastrophe Living by Jon Kabat-Zinn (Piatkus, £24.99)
